figures.shows: Three side-by-side diagrams of vertebrate circulatory systems, each with blue vessels (deoxygenated blood) on the left and red vessels (oxygenated blood) on the right, and arrows showing the direction of blood flow. The left diagram is labelled gill capillaries at the top, body capillaries at the bottom, and artery, heart and vein. Its heart is a single pumping chamber on the left side, and blood passes through the gill capillaries and then the body capillaries in a single loop. The middle diagram is labelled lung and skin capillaries at the top, body capillaries at the bottom, and artery, heart and vein. Its heart is drawn with mixed blue and red colouring, and the blood forms two loops, one to the lung and skin capillaries and one to the body. The right diagram is labelled lung capillaries at the top, body capillaries at the bottom, and artery, heart and vein. It has two loops like the middle diagram, but its heart is drawn with separate blue and red sides.
figures.original:

different vertebrate animals, then discuss the questions.

human circulatory system?

circulatory system? Explain this to a partner.

figures.shows: Three side-by-side diagrams of vertebrate circulatory systems, with blue vessels for blood with little oxygen and red vessels for blood with more oxygen. Two people in light shirts and blue caps, one wearing a face mask and white gloves, lean over the body and touch it. Other people stand behind a blue rope barrier in the background.
figures.original: With a partner, discuss why Yuka's body has been preserved for so long. Be ready to share your ideas with the rest of the class.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A model of a helium atom. At the centre is a nucleus of four touching spheres: two red spheres each marked with a plus sign and two grey spheres. A dashed circle around the nucleus is the orbit, and two small blue spheres, each marked with a minus sign, sit on it at the top right and the bottom left. There are no printed labels.
figures.original: Copy the diagram of a helium atom and label it, using these labels.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A line graph of average global temperature in °C (y-axis, 5 to 25) against millions of years ago (x-axis, from 400 on the left to 0 'today' on the right). The temperature starts near 23.5 °C at 400 million years ago and falls to about 10 °C by about 350 million years ago. It stays near 10 °C until about 260 million years ago, then rises sharply to about 24.5 °C at about 245 million years ago. It then declines to about 17 °C at about 190 million years ago, rises to about 24 °C from about 150 to 80 million years ago, falls to about 12 °C by about 15 million years ago, and rises slightly to about 12.7 °C today.
figures.original: The graph shows the average global temperatures over the past 400 million years.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A plane mirror is drawn as a vertical hatched line on the left, labelled 'plane mirror'. An incoming ray with an arrow travels from the upper right down to a point on the mirror. A reflected ray with an arrow leaves that point toward the lower right. A horizontal dashed line (the normal) meets the mirror at the same point. Angle A is between the mirror and the incoming ray, B is between the incoming ray and the normal, C is between the normal and the reflected ray, and D is between the reflected ray and the mirror.
figures.original: Which of the angles in this diagram is the angle of reflection?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A ray diagram with a straight arrowed line labelled "incident ray" sloping downward to the right toward a horizontal plane mirror. The plane mirror is drawn as a long horizontal line with hatching underneath and is labelled "plane mirror". The incident ray stops above the mirror and does not touch it. No normal, reflected ray or angles are drawn.
figures.original: Copy this ray diagram. You do not have to measure angles for making your copy.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A plane mirror is drawn as a hatched horizontal line at the top of the figure. A candle with a small flame is at the lower left, and Sofia, a cartoon girl with red hair, is at the lower right, drawn upside down. No light rays are drawn, so the diagram is incomplete.
figures.original: Sofia looks at a candle in the mirror. Copy and complete the diagram to show how light from the candle reflects from the mirror to Sofia.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A side-view diagram with a vertical line labelled 'wall' on the left and a horizontal line labelled 'floor' at the bottom. A rectangle labelled 'bed' sits above the floor to the right. A small triangle-shaped figure labelled 'Marcus' is at the top left, near the wall. A pencil lies on the floor at the bottom right, and a straight ray with an arrowhead runs from the pencil up and to the left, passing under the bed and ending in the space between the bed and the wall.
figures.original: Copy and complete the diagram by adding a mirror and a reflected light ray to show how Marcus can see the pencil.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of apparatus on a sheet of white paper. A mirror stands upright on two lumps of modelling clay at the far edge of the paper. A ray box connected to a power supply sends a ray, drawn as an arrow, towards the mirror. A pencil, a protractor and a ruler lie at the front right.
figures.original: Set up the equipment as shown in the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A ray diagram with a horizontal line marking the boundary between air (labelled above the line) and glass (labelled below the line). A straight ray of light labelled "ray of light" comes from the upper left, slopes down to the right, and has an arrowhead pointing towards the boundary. The ray stops where it meets the boundary. There is no normal line, and no ray is drawn inside the glass.
figures.original: This ray diagram shows a ray of light in air. Copy and complete the ray diagram to show what happens when the ray of light enters the glass.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A horizontal line separates the region labelled 'air' above from the region labelled 'water' below. A straight ray of light, labelled 'ray of light', travels upward and to the right through the water and meets the boundary. An arrowhead on the ray points up and to the right toward the boundary. The ray stops at the boundary, and nothing is drawn in the air.
figures.original: This diagram shows a ray of light in water. Copy and complete the ray diagram to show what happens when the ray of light enters the air.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A side-view drawing of an empty, straight-sided cup that is wider at the top, standing on a flat surface. A coin lies on the inside base of the cup and is labelled. A single straight line starts at the edge of the coin and slopes up to the right, passing the cup's right wall at the top of the picture. The cup is labelled.
figures.original: Can you use a ray diagram to explain why? You need to think about how a light ray travels from the coin, up through the water and out into the air.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of a glass tumbler containing water, standing on a flat surface, with a red pencil leaning in it. The pencil's tip rests at the bottom of the glass and its top sticks out above the water. The pencil looks broken or shifted where it crosses the water surface. The glass is labelled 'glass' and the water is labelled 'water'.
figures.original: Can you use a ray diagram to explain why? You need to think about how light travels from the pencil, through the water and out through the side of the glass.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A view from above of apparatus on a bench. A large sheet of white paper has a rectangular glass block in its middle. A ray box, connected by a wire to a power supply, sends a ray with an arrow towards the glass block. A pencil, a protractor and a 30 cm ruler lie to the right of the paper.
figures.original: Set up the equipment as shown in the diagram. The diagram shows the equipment viewed from above.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A line drawing of a triangular prism in perspective. It has two triangular faces at the ends and three rectangular faces along its length. Some hidden edges are faintly visible. There are no labels or values.
figures.original: The diagram shows a glass block used to separate white light. What name describes this piece of equipment?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A ray box, drawn as a rectangle, sends a thin incident ray up and to the right. An arrow on the ray points toward a triangular glass prism, and the ray meets the left side of the prism. On the right, a vertical line labelled screen stands some distance from the prism.
figures.original: Adjust the positions of the ray box and the screen until you see the colours of the rainbow on the screen.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A close-up photograph of bunches of cut flowers wrapped in clear and purple cellophane. The main flowers are a large orange zinnia and a red-orange zinnia, with yellow flowers and yellow buds on thin green stalks, purple-blue salvia spikes, pink and red cockscomb flowers, pink feathery celosia, and green leaves. White and pale pink flowers are blurred in the background.
figures.original: Make a list of all the colours you can see in this picture of flowers.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A screenshot of a computer colour picker window titled 'Colours' with the 'RGB Sliders' option selected. The Red slider is set to 255, Green to 0 and Blue to 255, the Hex Colour # is FF00FF, and Opacity is 100%. A pink/magenta colour swatch is shown at the bottom with Cancel and OK buttons.
figures.original: Try making: magenta, cyan, white, black. Now make some other colours of your choice. In each case, write down the RGB settings for each colour.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: Three panels show a blue cube and a red cube side by side. In white light (white background) the left cube is blue and the right cube is red. In blue light (blue background) the blue cube looks blue and the red cube looks black. In red light (red background) the blue cube looks black and the red cube looks red.
labels: blue and red cubes seen in white light
blue and red cubes seen in blue light
blue and red cubes seen in red light
figures.original: Look at the two cubes in the diagrams.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A vertical line is the boundary between air on the left and glass on the right. A single straight ray with an arrowhead comes from the upper left, travels downward to the right and stops at the boundary. No normal line and no angles are drawn.
figures.original: Copy these ray diagrams to show what happens to the light rays.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A horizontal line is the boundary between air (labelled above the line, at the right) and water (labelled below the line, at the right). A single straight ray with an arrowhead travels upward and to the right through the water and meets the boundary. No continuing ray in the air and no reflected ray is drawn, and no normal line is shown.
figures.original: Copy these ray diagrams to show what happens to the light rays.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A horizontal arrow labelled "white light" points to the right toward a vertical red bar labelled "red filter". A point labelled "A" is on the right side of the filter.
figures.original: a

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A horizontal arrow labelled 'white light' points right toward a thin vertical green bar labelled 'green filter'. The letter B is printed just to the right of the filter.
figures.original: b

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A black arrow labelled "white light" points from the left towards a blue vertical filter. To the right of it is a red vertical filter, with the letter C printed beside it. The filters are labelled "blue filter" and "red filter" underneath.
figures.original: c

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A horizontal plane mirror is drawn at the bottom as a line with hatching underneath it. A dashed vertical normal line rises from the mirror's surface. A single ray with an arrowhead comes from the upper left, slopes down to the right, and meets the mirror at the point where the normal touches it. No reflected ray is drawn.
figures.original: Copy and complete the diagram to show how light is reflected from the plane mirror.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A first-person photograph from a motorcycle or scooter rider's viewpoint, looking along a dirt road. Two round rear-view mirrors on stalks sit on the left and right of the handlebars, and each reflects part of the scene behind the rider. A round speedometer with a dial numbered 0 to 140 sits in the centre. The rider's left hand grips the handlebar.
figures.original: Draw a ray diagram to show how the rider can see a ray of light that is coming from behind.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table with three column headings: 'Food', 'Colour of iodine solution after adding to the food' and 'Does the food contain starch?'. Below the headings are two empty rows, and the bottom edge is a wavy line.
labels: Colour of iodine solution after adding to the food
figures.original: Draw a results table like this:

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A bar chart of the number of megajoules of energy needed each day by six people. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 12 in steps of 2. The bars are: baby aged 3 months 2, child aged 8 years 8, boy aged 15 years 11, girl aged 15 years 9, man aged 50 years 10, woman aged 50 years 8.
labels: Number of megajoules of energy needed each day
figures.original: The bar chart shows some examples of the energy that different people need each day. A megajoule (MJ) is one million joules.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A bar chart with three yellow bars showing the percentage of babies born with low birthweight for different numbers of cigarettes smoked per day by the mother during pregnancy. The bar for none is about 3.5, the bar for less than 15 is 8, and the bar for 15 or more is 9. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 10 in steps of 2.
labels: Percentage of babies born with low birthweight
Number of cigarettes per day smoked by mother during pregnancy
figures.original: Use the information in the bar chart to answer these questions.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A burger on a white plate. A bun holds a cooked meat patty flecked with herbs, a slice of pale yellow cheese, a ring of red onion, a slice of tomato and green rocket leaves. Thick-cut fried potato chips (fries) lie around the burger on the plate.
figures.original: Your little brother's favourite meal is a lamb burger and fries, with a sweet milky drink.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A labelled diagram of the arm bones and muscles. The scapula, humerus, radius and ulna are shown, with the biceps muscle on the front of the humerus and the triceps muscle on the back. The biceps has two tendons at its upper end and the triceps has three tendons at its upper end.
figures.original: The biceps is attached to the scapula at one end. Which bone is the other end attached to?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A labelled drawing of a human skeleton in a walking pose, with one leg raised and bent at the knee. Lines point to the cranium, vertebral column, clavicle, scapula, sternum, humerus, rib, ulna, radius, pelvic girdle, carpals, femur, tibia and fibula. The caption reads 'The human skeleton'.
figures.original: Look at the diagram of the skeleton. If you have a model of a skeleton, you could look at that as well.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A sequence of four images of the same man in a golf swing, set against a black background. He wears a red and grey cap, a white short-sleeved shirt, light grey trousers and a glove. In the first image his arms and club are raised on the backswing. In the second his arms are bent and the club points upward. In the third he is bringing the club down toward the ball with his arms extended. In the fourth he has finished the swing with the club behind his shoulders and his body turned.
figures.original: These pictures show a man hitting a golf shot. a Which hinge joints is he moving? b Which ball-and-socket joints is he moving?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A line graph of mean mass in kg (vertical axis, 10 to 60 in steps of 10) against age in years (horizontal axis, 2 to 20 in steps of 2). A smooth blue curve starts at about 12 kg at age 2, rises steadily to about 25 kg at age 8, rises steeply to about 48 kg at age 14, then levels off to about 58 kg at age 20.
figures.original: The graph shows the mean mass of girls at different ages.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A side-view drawing of a cat skeleton over a grey silhouette of the cat, facing left. Letters with label lines point to parts of the skeleton: D at the shoulder joint of the front leg, S at the upper front leg bone, P at the back of the upper front leg, R at the lower front leg, C at the front leg joint (elbow or wrist region), Q at the lower front leg or paw bones, A at the hip joint at the top of the back leg, and B at the knee joint of the back leg. A blue arrow near the front leg points up and to the left.
figures.original: The diagram shows the skeleton of a cat. Cats have the same bones as humans, but their sizes are different.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table titled "Sofia's results" with two columns: "Start temperature in °C" and "End temperature in °C". The single data row shows a start temperature of 18 and an end temperature of 42.
figures.original: Marcus thought that more chemical energy had been changed to thermal energy by his reaction because, in his experiment, the end temperature was higher. Sofia thought that both reactions changed the same quantity of chemical energy to thermal energy. Whose idea is correct? Explain why?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table titled "Marcus's results" with two columns: "Start temperature in °C" and "End temperature in °C". The single row of data shows a start temperature of 21 and an end temperature of 45.
figures.original: Marcus thought that more chemical energy had been changed to thermal energy by his reaction because, in his experiment, the end temperature was higher. Sofia thought that both reactions changed the same quantity of chemical energy to thermal energy. Whose idea is correct? Explain why?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: Three archery targets labelled A, B and C, each with concentric rings of yellow, red, blue, black/grey and white. On target A, three arrows are spread widely: one at the top right edge, one in the blue ring on the left, and one at the lower right in the blue/grey area. On target B, three arrows are tightly grouped in the yellow centre and the inner red ring. On target C, three arrows are tightly grouped at the upper left outer edge, outside the coloured rings.
figures.original: Look at these three archery targets.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: On the left is a cube of blue particles packed in a regular arrangement, labelled 'ice'. Three red arrows point at the cube from above and from both sides, and the text 'energy taken in' sits above the top arrow. A black arrow points right to a flat, spread-out, irregular layer of blue particles labelled 'water'.
figures.original: Why is ice melting called an endothermic process and not an endothermic reaction?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A hand in a blue sleeve holds a small wire loop or metal holder in the top of the blue flame of a Bunsen burner. The burner stands on a round base and is connected to an orange gas tube. No labels are printed.
figures.original: What safety precautions did you take?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: Four test tubes, each holding an iron nail, are shown at the start and again after a few weeks. Tube 1 is open with just a nail. Tube 2 is open with a nail partly in water. Tube 3 is stoppered with a nail above white lumps at the bottom. Tube 4 is stoppered with a nail in water that has a thin layer of oil on top. After a few weeks the nails in tubes 1 and 2 are covered in orange-brown rust, with tube 2 looking the most rusted, and the nails in tubes 3 and 4 look unchanged.
labels: After a few weeks the experiment looks like this.
figures.original: 5 Which test tube and which conditions caused the iron to rust most quickly?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed 'Tube number', 'Contains' and 'Result'. Four rows: tube 1 contains moist air and the nail is rusted; tube 2 contains water and air and the nail is very rusty; tube 3 contains dry air and there is no rust; tube 4 contains boiled water covered with oil, no air, and there is a small amount of rust.
labels: boiled water covered with oil, no air
figures.original: 4 What conditions are needed to prevent iron from rusting?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A wooden rack holds five test tubes containing clear liquid, each with a small piece of metal at the bottom. The first tube has only a few bubbles. The second has a moderate number of small bubbles. The third has a single column of larger bubbles. The fourth and fifth are filled with many bubbles, and the fourth has the most. No labels or values are printed.
figures.original: Record your observations in a table and explain what happened. You may need to leave the metal to react for some time. If nothing happens, you could try testing the metal again, this time using hot water.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of apparatus: a horizontal test tube with a piece of magnesium ribbon in the middle and ceramic wool at the closed end. A red arrow labelled 'heat' points up at the tube under the magnesium ribbon. The open end has a bung with a delivery tube through it, and hydrogen gas is burning at the tube's outer end. The caption is 'Heating magnesium'.
figures.original: Explain, using particle theory, why the reaction between steam and magnesium is more vigorous than between water and magnesium.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A beaker of water with a small piece of metal (calcium) resting on the bottom under an upturned funnel. A test tube filled with water is held upside down over the funnel stem, with bubbles of gas rising from the metal through the funnel into the tube. The labels point to the bubbles of gas, the water and the metal (calcium).
figures.original: What is the gas that is given off? How would you test for it?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of heating apparatus. A glass beaker containing water sits on a wire gauze on top of a tripod, with a thermometer standing in the water. Below the tripod is a lit spirit burner. The labelled parts are the thermometer, water, spirit burner and fuel in spirit burner.
figures.original: Burning is a chemical reaction where thermal energy is given out to the surroundings. Marcus has four fuels to investigate to find out which gives out the most thermal energy to the surroundings. He uses apparatus like this:

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: Five test tubes labelled A, B, C, D and E stand in a wooden rack, each containing a clear liquid with a small piece of metal at the bottom. Tube A has very few bubbles, tube B has a moderate number of bubbles, and tube C has a thin line of a few bubbles. Tubes D and E are densely filled with bubbles, with D having the most bubbles and E slightly fewer.
figures.original: 3 Which metal was the most reactive in dilute acid?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table with four columns: mass of calcium added in g, start temperature in °C, final temperature in °C, and temperature change in °C. There are four rows of data, with calcium masses of 1, 2, 3 and 4 g, a start temperature of 19 °C in every row, and final temperatures of 20, 21, 22 and 23 °C. The temperature change column is empty.

figures.original: Complete the table for both of the student's results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table with four columns: Mass of calcium added in g, Start temperature in °C, Final temperature in °C, and Temperature change in °C. There are four rows, for 1 g, 2 g, 3 g and 4 g of calcium. The start temperature is 21 in every row, and the final temperatures are 22, 22, 24 and 25. The Temperature change column is empty.
labels: Mass of calcium added in g
figures.original: Complete the table for both of the student's results.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A cartoon-style drawing of a school science laboratory with several students in unsafe situations. One student runs across the room. Two students at a bench with a microscope push each other, and a knife lies on a sheet of paper at the table edge. At another bench a student in a blue headscarf appears to taste or sniff a substance while a student in a tie leans over a bottle. A beaker lies on its side with liquid spilling onto the table and a puddle on the floor. A student at the side bench touches a lit Bunsen burner with the gas tubing loose, and a heated beaker on a tripod has a flame beside it. A girl at the front appears startled with her arms out. A tap and sink with a kettle are at the left.
figures.original: Start by looking carefully at the picture and identify as many things that are unsafe as you can. Make a list, with reasons, to explain why each thing is unsafe.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book

Curved lines of filings run outward from these clusters, and the filings are sparse and scattered near the top, bottom and edges. There are no labels.
figures.original: Where is the magnetic field strongest?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book

figures.original: Copy this diagram of a bar magnet.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of a wooden retort-style stand with a vertical rod on a flat wooden base and a horizontal wooden arm near the top, held by two clamps. A thread hangs from the arm and holds a paper strip sling under a bar magnet. The magnet hangs horizontally, with one half colored blue and the other half colored red. No labels or values are printed.
figures.original: Make a paper support for the bar magnet so that the magnet will hang horizontally, as shown in the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book

figures.original: Hold the needle or nail and gently stroke the bar magnet along it several times. as shown in the diagram.

figures.original: Set the needle on the disc and float the disc in the water, in a non-magnetic bowl, as shown.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
figures.shows: Four circuit diagrams labelled A, B, C and D. Each has a battery, an open switch and a coil of wire wrapped around a core in series. The core materials are labelled rubber (A), wood (B), nickel (C) and aluminium (D).
figures.original: The diagrams show circuit diagrams for four electromagnets. Each has the same current and the same number of turns in the coils. The material of the core is shown on each diagram. Which of the circuit diagrams will make the strongest electromagnet? Write one letter.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book

figures.original: Copy the diagram of two south poles from different magnets.

At 20 cm the counts are 28, 29 and 27. At 40 cm they are 19, 33 and 18. At 60 cm they are 12, 14 and 13. At 80 cm they are 8, 10 and 10.
labels: Distance of lamp from plant in cm
figures.original: Which is the anomalous result in Sofia's table?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.original: Explain why it was best to use a water plant in this experiment.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
figures.shows: A diagram of the Sun on the right and the Earth on the left, with a blue band labelled 'atmosphere' around the Earth. Three red lines run from the Sun toward the Earth. Two of them are marked with the number 1 and end at the Earth's surface. The third hits the surface, turns upward and is marked 2, then reaches a point in the atmosphere. There it splits into one line going up and out to space, marked 3, and one line going back toward the Earth, marked 4.
figures.original: With a partner, match each of these statements to one of the numbers on the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
figures.shows: A carbon cycle diagram with four blank rounded boxes labelled A, B, C and D. A sits at the top, B is beside the tree on the right, C is on a cow in the centre, and D is at the left above a petrol pump, coal and a gas cylinder. Arrows run from A to B (numbered 1) and from B back to A (labelled respiration). Arrows also run from the cow to A (respiration), from D to A (numbered 2), and from A to C via an arrow numbered 3. Arrows from B and C labelled 'urine, faeces, death' lead to a circle of microorganisms, which has an arrow to A. A long arrow from B labelled 'death and long-term subjection to high pressures and temperatures' leads to the fuels gasolene, coal and gas.
labels: death and long-term subjection to high pressures and temperatures
figures.original: Match each of these labels to the correct letter on the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
figures.shows: A drawing of apparatus: a beaker of sea water holds an upside down funnel with a piece of seaweed inside it. The narrow stem of the funnel leads into a measuring cylinder that stands upside down in the water and has a scale and small bubbles rising inside. figures.original: A school classroom has six identical lamps. Each of the lamps is connected in parallel across a 220 V mains supply, as shown in the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.original: Zara has a series circuit with a 9 V battery, a lamp and a buzzer as shown in the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

In A, the ammeter, voltmeter and lamp are all in series on one wire. In B, a voltmeter is in series with a parallel pair: the lamp and an ammeter in a branch above it. In C, an ammeter is in series with the lamp, and a voltmeter is in a branch in parallel with the lamp. In D, the lamp is on the main wire, with the ammeter in a parallel branch above it and the voltmeter in a parallel branch below it.
figures.original: Sofia wants to measure the current through a lamp and the voltage across the lamp. Which of these shows the correct way to do this? Write one letter.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.original: Set up the circuit as shown in the first diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.original: This circuit contains a 6Ω resistor. The current through the resistor is 2 A. Calculate the voltage across this resistor. Show your working and give the unit with your answer.

figures.original: This circuit contains a 100Ω resistor. The voltage across the resistor is 12 V. Calculate the current through this resistor. Show your working and give the unit with your answer.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.original: Set up the circuit with one cell as shown in the diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
figures.shows: A table with four cells, each describing a circuit to be drawn. Circuit 1: two lamps can be switched on and off separately, and the current through one of the lamps can be measured. Circuit 3: a fixed resistor and a variable resistor in series, and the voltage across the variable resistor can be measured. figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.original: Look at the circuit diagram.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book

figures.original: Calculate the reading on ammeter A1

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A close-up photograph of a clownfish with orange and yellow coloring and white bands edged in black. It is swimming among the pale purple-pink tentacles of a sea anemone. No text or labels are printed on it.
figures.original: Which photos show things that are alive?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A red-orange vintage Volkswagen Beetle car with red wheels is parked on a paved quayside beside water. Boats are moored in the background, and palm trees grow along the far shore.
figures.original: Which photos show things that are non-living?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A photograph of a landscaped garden with green lawn, two large olive trees with thick gnarled trunks and spreading branches, and a small stream edged with stones and rocks. Shrubs and flowering plants with green leaves and red, yellow and white flowers grow in beds beside the lawn, and white spherical lamps sit on the grass.
figures.original: Look at this garden. There are many different plants in this garden. Can you see a leaf? Can you see a flower? Can you see a stem? Can you see any roots?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Eight cartoon-style cards with coloured backgrounds, in two rows of four. The top row shows a brown hen on blue, a spotted cheetah on pale blue, four grey tadpoles on red, and a yellow chick on yellow. The bottom row shows two yellow spotted cheetah cubs on red, a white goat with horns on lime green, a green spotted frog on purple, and a white kid (young goat) on lilac.
figures.original: Can you match each adult animal with its young?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A cartoon drawing of four children looking at a red and white checked tablecloth covered with foods. The foods include a pineapple, a bottle of dark fizzy drink, butter, an apple, an orange, corn on the cob, a jug labelled CREAM, a bowl of rice, two spiky green fruits cut in half, a roast chicken leg, a bar of chocolate, a burger, a fish, a bowl labelled SUGAR, a jar labelled JAM, and a plate of chips.
figures.original: Which of these foods are healthy foods?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Two side-by-side drawings of environments. The left shows a desert with a bright sun in a blue sky, sand dunes, and a small rock with a spiky plant beside it. The right shows a pond of light blue water surrounded by green grass, reeds, cattails and yellow flowers. No animals are drawn in either picture.
figures.original: Which animals live in each environment?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Eight cartoon-style drawings of animals, in two rows of four, each in a coloured box with its name printed underneath. The top row shows a meerkat, a duck, a frog and a newt. The bottom row shows a snake, a scorpion, a dragonfly and a camel.
figures.original: Which animals live in each environment?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A colored drawing of a tomato plant growing in brown soil. It has a central stem with green leaves, several red tomatoes, one green unripe tomato, and a yellow flower with buds near the top. White branching roots spread underground. No labels or label lines are printed on it.
figures.original: Can you name the parts of this plant? Use these words.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A photograph of a field of maize (corn) plants that are dry, yellow and brown, with drooping, withered leaves. The soil is bare, dry and cracked, and the sky above is blue with a few white clouds. The photo sits in a round frame with a red border.
figures.original: What do these plants need?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A close-up photograph of many bean sprouts growing in a small round brown pot. The sprouts have long, thin, pale white stems and small yellow leaves at the top. Brown seed coats and seeds are visible at the base of the pot. The background is plain light grey and the photo sits inside a purple circle.
figures.original: What do these plants need?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A field of many sunflowers with yellow petals and brown centres, all turned to face the same direction towards the viewer. Green leaves and stems are visible below the flowers, and more sunflower rows stretch into the distance. A smooth yellow curved shape covers the bottom of the picture.
figures.original: Why are these plants all facing the same way?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A row of five photographs of young children. From left to right: a smiling girl with dark hair in two bunches, wearing a pink patterned jumper and holding a red toy; a boy with short dark curly hair sitting barefoot on a mat, stacking coloured blocks; colourful stacked blocks; a smiling boy with short dark brown hair and a teal top, peeking out from behind the blocks; a smiling girl with long light brown hair resting her chin on her hands. A yellow wave shape runs along the bottom.
figures.original: Look at these children. They are different. Which child has dark hair? Which children have brown eyes? Which children are girls?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Three hands are drawn with the fingers spread. One is pale cream, one is light brown or tan, and one is dark brown. Each hand has five fingers with nails. The pale hand is at the top left, the tan hand is at the right, and the dark brown hand is at the bottom. The hands are shown at different angles. The pale hand has a wrist and part of an arm, and the dark hand has a wrist.
figures.original: How are the hands the same? How are the hands different?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A table with two columns headed 'Hair colour' and 'Number of children'. The hair colour column has three cartoon faces: a girl with dark black curly hair, a girl with pale yellow hair in bunches, and a girl with golden yellow hair in plaits. The number column has red tick marks: 5 ticks for the black curly hair, 1 tick for the pale yellow hair, and 4 ticks for the golden plaited hair.
figures.original: How many children have red hair? Which colour is most common?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Four separate objects are drawn in a row. From left to right they are a yellow tub of margarine with the word 'margerine' printed on its lid, a grey metal key, a green glass bottle with no cap, and a yellow table with four legs.
figures.original: What materials are used to make these objects?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Four separate colored drawings of everyday objects in a row: a red car, a cream-colored cup or bucket with a white rim, a window with a yellow frame and three light blue glass panes, and a yellow wooden door with a round knob. There are no labels.
figures.original: Why are these objects made from these materials?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Eight colour drawings of everyday objects are spread over the page: a green glass bottle, a brown bottle labelled 'Cola', a grey spoon, a folded newspaper headed 'DAILY NEWS', a white metal food can with a ring pull, a beige disposable cup, a pink drinks can labelled 'FIZZ', and a white patterned plate.
figures.original: How could you sort these objects?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A cutaway cartoon drawing of a two-storey house. Upstairs on the left is a bedroom with a bookshelf with books, a yellow chest of drawers with books on top, a cardboard box, a rug with a pair of shoes and red socks, a bed with a green jumper, a blue dressing gown hanging on the wall and a lamp. Upstairs on the right is a bathroom with a purple bath, a shower curtain with fish on it, a basin with taps, a radiator, a sponge, a window and a black and white tiled floor. Downstairs on the left is a living room with a red armchair, a fireplace with a clock, a round wooden table with a plastic water bottle and a milk bottle, a newspaper and magazine, and a cardboard box. Downstairs on the right is a kitchen with cupboards, a cooker with a saucepan, a sink, a mug, an electric kettle, a washing machine and a cooker hood.
figures.original: What materials can you see? Are they strong? Are they flexible? Are they warm or soft to the touch? Can you see through them?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Four cartoon-style drawings of toys, each on its own coloured square. Top left is a yellow toy truck with a brown open box at the back, blue wheels and a tall blue push handle. Top right is a toy train with a green engine, a red funnel, one yellow carriage with a blue roof and red wheels, and a second carriage joined behind it. Bottom left is a pink child's bicycle with a basket behind the seat, small stabiliser wheels at the back and ribbons on the handlebars. Bottom right is a yellow wooden giraffe on red wheels with a string trailing from the back.
figures.original: Which toys do you pull? Which toys do you push?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A woman astronaut inside a space station is floating in mid-air with no support from the floor. She wears a blue jacket and blue trousers and white socks. One hand holds a horizontal bar on the ceiling above her, and her body and legs float sideways. Equipment, cables and panels fill the background.
figures.original: Moving in space can be hard. How is the astronaut moving?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: A cartoon drawing of a woman in a pink shirt and black trousers walking behind a pushchair and holding its handles with both hands. A baby in a hat and striped clothes sits in the blue pushchair and waves one hand. The woman is behind the pushchair and leans slightly forward as the pushchair moves ahead of her.
figures.original: Is she pulling or pushing?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Four circular photographs with coloured borders show people moving. One shows a woman in a blue and red traditional dress spinning in a dance. One shows a horse pulling a two-wheeled cart with passengers along a road. One shows a girl swinging from a rope above snowy ground. One shows a man in a helmet and sunglasses pushing a racing wheelchair along a road.
figures.original: How are these people moving? Can you find turning, swinging, pushing and pulling?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 1 Learner’s Book
figures.shows: Eight colored picture cards in two columns and four rows. The cards show: a light blue car with exhaust puffs, a pink flower in a brown pot, a red balloon with ribbons, an open book with text and a picture of a camel, a bed with a red blanket and white pillow, a brown horse standing, a red electric guitar, and a television screen.
figures.original: Which of these make sounds you can hear?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
figures.shows: Three cartoon drawings labelled A, B and C show environmental problems. A shows a park path and grass covered in litter such as bottles, cans and paper, with a bin at the top left. B shows a tree with a broken branch, tied to a wooden post. C shows a pond or stream with rubbish in the water, including a tyre, a fishing net, a can, a bottle and a fish skeleton.
figures.original: What could we do to solve the problems in these environments?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
figures.shows: A block graph (bar chart) of rain on each day from Monday to Friday. The vertical axis has four levels labelled, from bottom to top: No rain, A little rain, A lot of rain, Rain all day. Monday, Wednesday and Friday have bars up to 'A little rain', Tuesday has a bar up to 'A lot of rain', and Thursday has no bar.
figures.original: Some learners measured the amount of rain each day and drew this block graph.

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
figures.shows: A satellite photograph of a large hurricane seen from above. White clouds swirl in a huge spiral around a small dark eye at the center. Dark blue sea surrounds the storm, with green land at the bottom left, the bottom right and the top right.
figures.original: Look at the picture. There is a very bad storm under these clouds. The storm is moving nearer the land. What will happen to the weather on the land?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
figures.shows: Two scenes are shown at the top. The left one, labelled 'dry place', shows a flat-topped tree on sandy ground under a bright sun. The right one, labelled 'wet place', shows a pond with lily pads, reeds and green bushes. Below are six labelled animal drawings: eagle, frog, duck, goat, lion and fish.
figures.original: Which animals might live in the dry place?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF

figures.original: Which place is best for minibeasts and plants to live in?

figures.original: Which do you think you can twist with your hands?

labels: Distance paper plane flew in metres
figures.original: Juno used different elastic bands to flick three identical paper aeroplanes.

figures.original: Which of these are light sources?

figures.original: Will the bulb be on or off in these circuits? Why?

figures.original: Try changing the bulb for a buzzer or motor. What do you think will happen?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF

Bottom right: a red rocker switch marked I and O, on a white extension socket with a white plug pushed in.
figures.original: What do you think these switches do?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF

They include a large black Vinnic 4R 25 6 volt lantern battery, two blue Ever Ready lantern-type batteries, a red Ever Ready Silver Seal cell, a blue Ever Ready cell, a black and gold Gold Seal cell, Kodak and Duracell 9 volt batteries, several smaller cylindrical cells including Duracell ones, and three small button cells at the bottom right.
figures.original: These have two names. What are they?

(d) is a switch with a black handle and a yellow lever on a flat base, with the lever raised and open.
figures.original: What are these called?

figures.original: Look at this picture of the Earth. Which part is day? Which part is night?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF

A tall, flat, triangular pointer (the gnomon) stands in the middle and casts a blue shadow across the plate towards the numbers 10 to 12. The tip of the shadow lies near the lines for 10 and 11, and the pointer itself lies near 12 and 1.
figures.original: Look at the picture. Can you tell what time it is?
