A red curve starts at the origin and rises steeply, then levels off at about 52-53 m/s by around 13 s and stays nearly constant to 20 s. A straight blue line starts at 20 m/s at 0 s and touches the red curve at about 5.5 s at roughly 42 m/s, reaching 70 m/s at 13 s. Black dashed lines mark 20 m/s horizontally from 0 to 13 s and 13 s vertically from 20 to 70 m/s.
figures.original: Look at Figure 2.20. What is the skydiver's acceleration at: a 0 s b 5.5 s?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table titled Table 2.8 with three columns: Station, Distance travelled/km, and Time taken/minutes. It lists five stations with their distances and times: Hornby 0 km, 0 min; Kirby Lonsdale 10 km, 30 min; Ingleton 20 km, 45 min; Dolphinholme 46 km, 60 min; Galgate 56 km, 80 min.
figures.original: Use the data in Table 2.8 to plot a distance–time graph for the train. Find the train's average speed between Kirby Lonsdale and Dolphinholme. Give your answer in km/h.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A ticker tape is drawn as two strips, one above the other, with a row of dots along each. Some dots are labelled with numbers: 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 on the upper strip, and 25 and 30 on the lower strip. The dots are very close together near 0 and get steadily further apart along the tape. After about 10 the spacing looks roughly even, and it stays even to the end at 30.
figures.original: Copy and complete Table 2.10, using the ticker tape to help you.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A speed–time graph with time in s on the horizontal axis (0 to 120, labelled every 20) and speed in m/s on the vertical axis (0 to 40, labelled every 10). The line rises in a straight line from 0 at time 0 to about 43 m/s at about 15 s, stays flat at that speed until about 95 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 at 120 s.
figures.original: How is a constant velocity shown on the graph?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A velocity–time graph with time in seconds on the horizontal axis (marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) and velocity on the vertical axis (no numbers given). A straight line rises from the origin to a peak at about 7.2 s, and a dashed vertical line drops from the peak to the time axis. A steeper straight line then falls from the peak to zero velocity at 10 s.
figures.original: The velocity–time graph shows the performance of a Formula 1® racing car as it accelerates from rest for 7.33 seconds and then brakes, coming to a stop in 2.69 seconds. It covers a distance of 520 metres. What is the approximate maximum velocity of the car?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Three separate objects, each with a thick green arrow showing the direction of a force. (a) A golf ball on a red tee with a green arrow pointing to the right. (b) A car drawn with speed lines behind it, with a green arrow at its front pointing to the left. (c) An aeroplane seen from above, with a green arrow pointing up and to the left, across the fuselage.
figures.original: Figure 3.7 shows three objects that are moving. A force acts on each object. For each, say how its movement will change.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A photograph of a hammer thrower in a red outfit and blue shoes, spinning inside a throwing circle. She holds the handle of the hammer, and the wire stretches out to the left. The circle is surrounded by a tall red-posted protective cage with netting, with a stadium and spectators behind it. A bib on her front reads 'WANG'.
figures.original: Throwing the hammer is an Olympic sport (Figure 3.15), where the thrower spins around inside a circle while swinging a 'hammer'. Throwers spin as fast as they can before releasing the hammer. Looking down from above, sketch the path of the hammer moving in a circle followed by its path after it is released.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed Force, Mass and Acceleration / m/s², and four rows. Row 1: Force a, mass 50 kg, acceleration 10. Row 2: force 112 N, mass 70 kg, acceleration b. Row 3: force 110 kN, mass c, acceleration 5. Row 4: force d, mass 15 g, acceleration 10. The letters a, b, c and d mark the missing values. The caption reads Table 3.3.
figures.original: Look at Table 3.3. Calculate the missing values a–d. Show your working.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A drawing of a tan wooden block, a long rectangular box, shown in perspective with its open end facing the lower left. A small green tennis ball sits at the lower left, and a black arrow runs from the ball to the block's end face, showing the ball travelling toward the block. There are no labels or values.
figures.original: Explain how the speed of the ball can be calculated using the principle of conservation of momentum. (Hint: this is a collision between the ball and the box.)

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four circles represent raindrops, labelled a, b, c and d, each with a vertical arrow pointing up from the top and a vertical arrow pointing down from the bottom. Drop a has 2.6 N up and 2.6 N down. Drop b has 1.4 N up and 1.8 N down. Drop c has 3.1 N up and 1.8 N down. Drop d has 0.8 N up and 2.6 N down.
figures.original: Which raindrop is slowing down?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A drawing of a spanner on a bolt head at its upper left end. A dashed line along the spanner from the bolt to the handle end is labelled 50 cm. A horizontal dashed line at the top is labelled 30 cm, and a vertical dashed line on the right is labelled 40 cm. A green arrow at the handle end points down and to the left and is labelled "force provided by man = 30 N".
figures.original: A bolt is tightened by applying a turning force of 30 N to the end of the spanner (Figure 4.8). a Which of the three distance measurements should you use? b Use this distance to calculate the moment.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal brown ruler rests on a red triangular pivot located at its midpoint. A downward green arrow labelled 90 N acts on the left part of the ruler, 0.18 m to the left of the pivot. A downward green arrow labelled F acts near the right end, 0.07 m to the right of the pivot. Dashed vertical lines mark the positions of the two forces and the pivot.
figures.original: A uniform metre ruler is balanced at its midpoint (Figure 4.9). Calculate the unknown force F.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A side view of a horizontal trapdoor set in a floor, with a hinge at its left end. Three upward forces act on it: F1 = 300 N is a vertical arrow near the hinge, F2 = 200 N is a long arrow at the far right end that slants up and to the left, and F3 = 200 N is a vertical arrow at the far right end. The hinge and the trapdoor are labelled below the figure.
figures.original: Three different forces are pulling on a heavy trapdoor (Figure 4.6). Which force will have the biggest turning effect? Explain your answer.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A red double-decker bus labelled 'bus A' is tilted on a sloping platform, leaning over at a steep angle. A star marks the centre of gravity on the bus, and a label points to it reading 'centre of gravity'. A long vertical line with small marks runs beside the bus down to a red dot at the base, where the platform meets the flat ground.
figures.original: Buses and other vehicles have to be tilt-tested to an angle of at least 28 degrees from the vertical before they can carry passengers.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A photograph of a man in a light blue robe and white head covering pulling down on a long pole attached to a wooden lever (a shaduf) beside a river. The long wooden beam rests on a wooden frame pivot, with a woven basket or bucket hanging from a rope at one end and a counterweight of clay or mud at the other. Trees and plants are in the background.
figures.original: What is the advantage of making it take as much effort to push the bucket down as it does to pull it up?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal brown ruler rests on a red triangular pivot. A 76 N downward force acts on the left side, 0.44 m to the left of the pivot. Two downward forces act on the right side: 125 N, drawn just to the right of the pivot, and 56 N, which is 0.34 m to the right of the pivot. The 0.44 m and 0.34 m distances are marked with dimension arrows between dashed vertical lines.
figures.original: Calculate the distance to the right of the pivot that the 125 N load needs to be placed for the ruler to be balanced.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal brown beam rests on a red triangular pivot located to the right of the beam's centre. A green block labelled 0.47 N hangs by a string from a point on the left part of the beam. The distance from the left end of the beam to the string is marked 0.13 m, and the distance from the left end to the pivot is marked 0.33 m, as shown by double-headed arrows.
figures.original: Calculate the anticlockwise moment of the 0.47 N force.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Three drawings, labelled A, B and C, show a person standing on a sailboard floating on water. In A the sail lies flat on the water and the person leans back, pulling a rope attached to it. In B the sail is partly raised and the person still leans back and pulls the rope. In C the sail is upright and the person stands almost upright holding the mast. A point P is marked on the board at the base of the sail in each drawing.
figures.original: a As the sail is pulled up from A to C, how does the force needed vary? Explain your answer.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A windsurfer stands on a board floating on wavy water, holding a sail. A horizontal arrow labelled 'wind force' points left from the sail, and a vertical double-headed arrow labelled '1.5 m' marks the height of that arrow above the pivot. The point P is marked on the board at the base of the mast, and a downward arrow labelled 'weight' acts from the board.
figures.original: c Calculate how far to the right of the pivot the windsurfer has to move his centre of gravity.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two drawings of an angle-poise lamp on a base. Each has a vertical stem with a pivot at the top, a lamp arm, and a cord running vertically down from the pivot to a spring near the base. In the left drawing the arm is horizontal, the lamp hangs at its left end, a 25 cm distance is marked from the line of the 3.75 N downward weight to the pivot, and in the right drawing the arm is tilted upward to the left with the lamp raised and a 3.75 N downward weight arrow. The vertical cord is labelled 'pivot' in both drawings.
figures.original: The diagram shows an angle-poise lamp. The light is at the end of an arm. The arm can be moved about the pivot. The cord passes vertically down to a stretched spring.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four panels (a, b, c, d) each show a bicycle chainring with a crank arm and pedal in a different position, with a downward force of 500 N on the pedal. In a, the pedal is up and to the left, with a 5 cm horizontal distance marked at the pedal and a 14 cm vertical distance marked near the crank. In b, the crank points straight up and is labelled 15 cm. In c, the crank points horizontally left and is labelled 15 cm. In d, the crank points left and slightly up, with 5 cm marked vertically at the pedal and 14 cm marked horizontally.
figures.original: The pictures show different positions of a bicycle pedal. Which position would result in the biggest turning force?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A plan view of a gate drawn as a long horizontal bar with a pivot at its left end, labelled 'pivot', and a block under each end. Four force arrows are labelled A, B, C and D. A is a short upward arrow close to the pivot. B is a medium-length upward arrow about halfway along the gate. C is a long arrow at the far right end, pointing up and to the left at an angle. D is the longest arrow, pointing straight up at the far right end.
figures.original: This is a plan view of a gate that will swing open about the pivot shown. Also shown are the positions for a motor and the direction they will move the gate. The length of the arrows indicates the size of the force. Choose the arrow that will swing the gate open the quickest.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal beam bridge rests on two pairs of sloping legs, one at the left end and one at the right end. A toy steam train sits on the bridge roughly midway between the supports. An upward arrow at the left support is labelled 'force X', and an upward arrow at the right support is labelled 'force Y'. A downward arrow from the train is labelled 'weight of train 8 N'.
figures.original: A toy train is crossing a bridge. The centre of gravity of the train is mid-way between the supports. Which row of the table shows the correct values of the contact forces at X and Y?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A horizontal bar (a ruler) is marked with a scale from 0 cm at the left end to 100 cm at the right end. A triangular pivot sits under the bar at the 55 cm mark. A 50 g mass hangs from a string looped around the bar at the 85 cm mark.
figures.original: A 1.0 metre wooden ruler is damaged and no longer uniform. The mass of the ruler is 11.5 g. The ruler is balanced on a pivot with a 50 g mass as shown. Where is the centre of gravity of the ruler?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two parts, a and b, show a cyclist seen from behind. In a, the cyclist is upright, with a green arrow labelled 'weight' pointing down and a green arrow labelled 'contact force' pointing up at the ground. In b, the cyclist leans to one side while turning, shown by a red dashed curved arrow. The arrows are 'weight' pointing down, 'contact force' pointing up and 'friction' pointing sideways along the ground.
figures.original: Figure 4.24 shows the forces acting on a cyclist.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table titled Table 5.2 with three columns: Load/N, Length/cm and Extension/cm. Load and length values are printed for nine rows, and the Extension column has 0 in the first row and is blank for all the other rows.
figures.original: Table 5.2 shows the results of an experiment to stretch an elastic cord. Copy and complete the table, and draw a graph to represent this data (with load on the vertical axis).

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two photographs labelled a and b show the same multicoloured bowl made of swirled orange, red, blue, yellow, green and white material, resting on a grey speckled surface. In a, the bowl is a regular, round, upright bowl. In b, the bowl has sagged and deformed into a flattened, saddle-like shape with a raised, wavy middle.
figures.original: Using your knowledge of physics, explain how this can happen.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with two columns headed 'Load/N' and 'Length/m'. It has six rows of values: 0.0 N with 1.396 m, 2.6 N with 1.422 m, 5.3 N with 1.448 m, 7.9 N with 1.475 m, 10.6 N with 1.501 m, and 13.2 N with 1.536 m.
figures.original: The results of an experiment to stretch a spring are shown in Table 5.3. Use the results to plot a load–extension graph. On your graph, mark the limit of proportionality and state the value of the load at that point.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A book held in two hands and bent into an arch, with the spine on the left and the page edges fanning out at the right end. The front cover is the outer, upper curved surface and the back cover is the inner, lower curved surface. A short red dashed line at the right end marks the difference in length between the front and back covers if the book were a solid block of paper.
labels: This would be the difference in length between the front and back covers if the book was a solid block of paper.
figures.original: Now bend it into the shape of an arch with the spine on the left-hand side as shown in Figure 5.11.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A car hydraulic braking system. A foot pushes a pedal connected to an effort piston in a cylinder, with an arrow showing the direction of push. Brake fluid in a pipe runs to a caliper with two load pistons on either side of a brake disc, with arrows pointing inwards. The brake disc is attached to an axle and the wheel with its tyre. A second pipe branches off labelled 'to other brakes'.
figures.original: Car braking systems multiply forces. In the diagram below, there are three pistons: one effort piston and two load pistons.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two drawings of a coil spring hung from a fixed support. On the left the spring hangs with nothing attached, and its length from the support is marked as 8 cm. On the right the spring hangs from the support with a cylindrical mass attached at the bottom, and its length is marked as 18 cm.
figures.original: This spring obeys Hooke's law and stretches from 8 cm to 18 cm when a force of 20 N is applied.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four table legs, labelled A, B, C and D, each drawn standing on a flat floor line. Leg A is a vertical leg that widens into a flared, bulging foot with a flat base. Leg B is a vertical leg that narrows and then spreads out into a wide, rounded flared base. Leg C is a leg that tapers to a narrow point at the floor. Leg D is a leg fitted with a small round castor wheel at the bottom.
figures.original: Heavy furniture sometimes marks the floor on which it stands. Four tables of the same weight each have four legs. The figure shows part of a leg from each table. Which table is least likely to mark the floor?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Four circles labelled A, B, C and D, each representing a submarine, with small arrows drawn around the outside. In A, the arrows all point inward toward the circle and are about the same length all the way round. In B, the arrows point inward, and those at the top and bottom are drawn slightly longer than the others. In C, the arrows point inward and are longer at the top and shorter at the bottom. In D, the arrows point inward and are longer at the bottom and shorter at the top.
figures.original: Which diagram shows the pressure acting on the submarine that is not moving?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A graph with Load / N on the vertical axis and Extension / cm on the horizontal axis. Four straight lines labelled A, B, C and D all start at the origin. A is the steepest, then B, then C, and D is the shallowest. No numerical values are printed on either axis.
figures.original: Look at the graph. Which material is the stiffest?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two tall open-topped containers labelled A and B stand side by side. Each has a tap at the bottom, and a pipe joins the two taps. A vertical double-headed arrow at the left of container A is labelled 80 cm and spans from the base up the side of the container. Container A appears empty. Container B has a faint line partway up, which may mark a water level.
figures.original: The diagram shows two containers that store rainwater. The containers have taps. A pipe joins the taps. The taps are closed. Both containers have a base of area 0.07 m².

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table titled 'ACTIVITY 6.3 Moon flight high jump' with columns: High jump record / m, Athlete, Height of athlete / m, Year. Men: 2.45, Javier Sotomayor (Cuba), 1.95, 1993. Women: 2.09, Stefka Kostadinova (Bulgaria), 1.80, 1987.
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: Table 6.4 lists the current world records for the high jump. Predict what the high jump record would be on the lunar surface.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A side-on drawing of a roller coaster track supported by a criss-cross lattice, with a small car at the bottom left on the upward slope. The track rises to a high peak P, falls to a low dip Q, rises to a smaller peak R, then falls to ground level at S. A double-headed arrow at P is labelled 50 m and shows the height of P above the ground. Another arrow at R shows the height of R above the ground and is labelled with a question mark.
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: This diagram shows an amusement park roller coaster ride (not drawn to scale).

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Five numbered panels (1 to 5) show an athlete at successive stages of a pole vault. Each panel has a vertical bar (the crossbar upright) and a light blue landing mat on the right. In 1 the athlete runs carrying a horizontal pole, in 2 the pole tip is planted at the base of the upright, in 3 the pole is bent with the athlete swinging upward, in 4 the pole is straight and upright as the athlete passes over the bar, and in 5 the athlete lies on the mat with the pole fallen on the ground.
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: Snapshots (labelled 1–5) of an athlete at different stages of the pole vault are as shown in Figure 6.17. Between each snapshot, the energy is transferred between stores.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: Two side-by-side drawings of a ballistic pendulum, labelled 'before' and 'after'. Before: a block hangs from a pivot on a vertical rod, and a small dot (the projectile) to its left moves right with speed labelled V_P. After: the projectile is embedded in the block, which swings up along a dashed outline to the right with speed labelled V_B, and the vertical rise of the block is marked as height h.
figures.original: Scientists use a ballistic pendulum to work out the speed of a projectile that hits it. The block has a mass of 4.7 kg and moves with an initial speed of 1.24 m/s when it is hit.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with three column headings: 'Description', 'Name of energy' and 'Store or transfer'. The Description column has eight filled-in rows, and the other two columns are empty for the learner to complete.
labels: energy carried by an electric current
energy in the nucleus of an atom
energy escaping from a hot object
figures.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
figures.original: Copy and complete the table. For each description, write down the name of the associated energy and state whether it is a store or transfer.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A Sankey-style energy transfer diagram. A wide grey arrow labelled 'energy input' on the left splits into two arrows: a wide arrow pointing right to 'useful energy output', and a thinner arrow curving downward to 'waste energy'.
figures.original: This diagram represents an energy transfer. Copy and complete the following two word equations for this energy change:

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A map of Sanghera Island with north arrow at top, showing contour-shaded hills with spot heights, streams, forest patches in the north, two hot springs, and dotted tracks. A scale bar shows 1 km. Spot heights are 278, 338, 571, 778 and 812.
figures.original: Sanghera Island (Figure 7.10) is a remote fictitious island.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with three columns headed 'Energy resource', 'Non-renewable' and 'Renewable'. The first column lists ten energy resources: wave power, hydroelectricity, geothermal, coal, nuclear energy, oil, solar energy, natural gas, tidal energy and wind energy. The Non-renewable and Renewable columns are empty.
figures.original: Copy the table. In the first blank column, put a tick by any three resources that are non-renewable. In the second blank column, put a tick by any three resources that are renewable.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with columns 'Type of power station', 'For', 'Against' and 'Overall score'. The wind farm row has For 2, Against 4 and Overall score −2. The nuclear row has For 7, Against 3 and Overall score 4.
figures.original: Subtract your vote for the opposition from your vote for the advocates to get an overall score. Two examples are given in Table 7.1.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A girl pushes a wooden box up a sloping ramp. A green arrow pointing right from the box is labelled 200 N, and a green arrow pointing straight down from the box is labelled 400 N. The ramp's sloping length is marked 2.5 m, and its vertical height is marked 0.75 m.
figures.original: a How much work does she do in raising the box? b How much g.p.e. does the box gain?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A washing machine sits on a straight wooden ramp that slopes upward to the right, from the ground to the floor of a trailer (removal van). A double-headed arrow along the ramp is labelled 1.6 m, and an arrow pointing up the slope is labelled 440 N. A vertical double-headed arrow on the trailer shows its floor height above the ground as 0.80 m.
figures.original: A man is trying to move his washing machine into the back of a removal van. The washing machine has a weight of 650 N and the floor of the removal van is 0.80 metres above the ground (Figure 8.9).

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A gymnast in a white sleeveless top and long white trousers holds himself motionless on two gymnastic rings, with his arms stretched out horizontally to each side and his body hanging straight down. Spectators sit in stands behind him. No labels or values are printed.
figures.original: But is he doing any work from a physics point of view?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A table with four columns: Speed / m/s, Thinking distance / m, Braking distance / m, Stopping distance / m. It has six rows: 8.9, 6, 6, 12; 13.4, 9, 14, 23; 17.9, 12, 24, 36; 22.3, 15, 38, 53; 26.8, 18, 55, 73; 31.3, 21, 75, 96.
figures.original: Assume that the mass of the car is 1500 kg and the braking force is 10 000 N. Show that you get nearly the same braking distance as in Table 8.1.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A brown horse on the left pulls a rope that runs up and over a spoked pulley wheel at the upper right. The rope's other end holds an orange block on the right. The block is drawn at two heights: a lower one labelled 33 000 lb and a higher one raised by Δh = 1 foot, with an upward arrow and a brace between them. A stopwatch symbol is labelled Δt = 1 min.
figures.original: 7 One horsepower is the power output of one horse when it lifts a mass of 33 000 lb of water through a height of one foot in one minute as shown in Figure 8.12.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A right-angled slope (incline) rising to the right, with a man pushing a pram up it. A 150 N arrow points up along the slope. The slope length is labelled 20 m with a double-headed arrow along the underside of the slope. The vertical height at the right-hand end is labelled 10 m with a double-headed arrow.
figures.original: A man pushes a 25 kg pram up a slope as shown in the diagram. He pushes with a force of 150 N along the 20 m slope. How much energy is dissipated as thermal energy?

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A cross-section of a subway station. A row of terraced houses stands at street level, and a vertical shaft with a people symbol runs from the street down to a train at the platform. The platform and train sit at a higher level than the tunnel on each side. The tunnel slopes down on both sides of the station to a lower level.
figures.original: The diagram shows a section through a subway station. The track at the station platform is designed to be higher up than the track in the tunnels. The driver uses brakes to stop the train at the platform and a motor to make the train set off. What is the advantage of having the platform higher up than the track in the tunnels? Explain your answer in terms of the work done by the brakes and the motor.

figures.textbookName: IGCSE-Physics-Coursebook-by-David-Sang
figures.shows: A drawing of a syringe tilted diagonally, with the needle tip at the upper right and the plunger with its flange at the lower left. figures.original: Find the area and perimeter of the following. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.

figures.original: How many of the students do not take maths or physics?

figures.textbookName: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
figures.shows: A parallelogram OABC with O at the bottom left, C at the bottom right, B at the top right and A at the top left. An arrow on OA is labelled p and points from O towards A, and an arrow on OC is labelled q and points from O towards C. Point E lies on the top side AB, nearer to B. The diagram is marked NOT TO SCALE.
figures.original: OABC is a parallelogram. OA = p and OC = q E is the point on AB such that AE : EB = 3 : 1. Find OE, in terms of p and q, in its simplest form.

figures.original: S is a point on PQ such that PS : SQ = 4 : 5. Find OS, in terms of a and b, in its simplest form.
